language_wrapper: A deck consists of cards described by {num_attributes} independent attributes. Each attribute can take one of {num_values} values, and every attribute-value combination appears exactly once, so the deck has {num_values}^{num_attributes} cards. A selection of {num_values} distinct cards is called complementary if, for every attribute, the values across the selected cards are either all identical or all pairwise distinct. Among all complementary selections of {num_values} cards, how many have exactly {exact_same_attrs} attributes that are identical across the selection?
teacher_generator_code:
def generator(rng):
    # Choose prime p >= 3 for number of values per attribute
    primes = [3, 5, 7, 11, 13]
    p = rng.choice(primes)
    # Choose number of attributes n >= 3
    n = rng.randint(3, 7)
    # Choose exact_same_attrs s between 1 and n-2 to avoid trivial extremes
    if n - 2 >= 1:
        s = rng.randint(1, n - 2)
    else:
        # Fallback, though for n>=3 this won't trigger
        s = 1
    return {
        'num_attributes': n,
        'num_values': p,
        'exact_same_attrs': s
    }
hardness_rationale: The seed problem counts all complementary triples when there are 3 attributes and 3 values, which can be solved by a straightforward ordered-pair argument. Our family generalizes to p values per attribute (p prime) and n attributes, and additionally constrains the exact number s of attributes that must be identical across the selection. Solving requires recognizing the affine geometry structure over GF(p)^n, classifying complementary sets as affine lines, and then refining the count by the zero-pattern of direction vectors to enforce exactly s identical attributes. This classification and the use of field-based reasoning is more advanced and not amenable to simple guessing.
notes: Proof outline: Model the deck as GF(p)^n, where each card is a vector of attribute values in GF(p). A complementary selection of p cards is precisely an affine line L = v0 + t·d (t in GF(p)) with direction d != 0, because on coordinates with d_i = 0 the attribute is constant ("all same"), and on coordinates with d_i != 0 the attribute cycles through all p distinct values ("all distinct"). Thus complementary selections of size p biject with affine lines in GF(p)^n. The number of distinct affine lines is p^{n-1} times the number of 1-dimensional subspaces (directions), which equals (p^n - 1)/(p - 1), reproducing the classic total count. To enforce exactly s attributes identical, we must count only those lines whose direction has exactly s zero coordinates. The number of direction subspaces with exactly s zeros is: choose the s zero coordinates (C(n, s)); assign nonzero field values to the remaining n - s coordinates ((p - 1)^{n - s}), and then factor by the p - 1 scalar multiples that generate the same 1D subspace, yielding C(n, s)·(p - 1)^{n - s - 1} subspaces. Each such direction produces p^{n-1} distinct affine lines (cosets). Therefore the total number of complementary selections with exactly s identical attributes is p^{n-1}·C(n, s)·(p - 1)^{n - s - 1}. This derivation relies on field properties and affine geometry over GF(p), ensuring correctness and making the solution more sophisticated than the seed.
source_question: Every card in a deck has a picture of one shape - circle, square, or triangle, which is painted in one of the three colors - red, blue, or green. Furthermore, each color is applied in one of three shades - light, medium, or dark. The deck has 27 cards, with every shape-color-shade combination represented. A set of three cards from the deck is called complementary if all of the following statements are true: i. Either each of the three cards has a different shape or all three of the card have the same shape. ii. Either each of the three cards has a different color or all three of the cards have the same color. iii. Either each of the three cards has a different shade or all three of the cards have the same shade. How many different complementary three-card sets are there?
